summary: We developed two ways to transform data into music. We made this by the use of spectrograms and Perlin noise model. For this, we utilized the API of the resources page and extracted the meta data from it in order to later transform this variables into a Perlin math function. This project addresses a critical accesibility challenge because it serves as a method for people with disabilities to have access to an auditory way of experiencing information they otherwise could not access.
details:
The group comprised of David Sanchez, Pablo Quiñonez, Luis Elias Felix, and Jose Angel Sebastian Hernandez, known as “Superbad,” participated in NASA Space Apps 2026 in Mexicali. The event took place at CETYS University, specifically in the Norberto Corella Gil Samaniego Library. Our team selected the Earth Information Jukebox, which involves converting images and graphic resources into audio format. Professor Lorena Marron served as our supervisor. Each member was assigned a specific task. The project aimed to enable people with disabilities, such as blindness, to identify graphics based on sound. Although this technology is still in its early stages, this project demonstrated its progress. It was also chosen because it allowed us to explore two areas of the visual arts in which two of our members were already familiar: photography and music.

Pablo Quiñonez took the initiative and was in charge of the overall plan, planning the use of platforms such as Requests, Pillow, Pandas, Reaper, and OpenCV. However, as we started our project, we realized the enormous challenges our team faced, such as the specialization of our members in a single area of ​​the project, the path we chose, and the goals each of us sought to achieve. Although we were soon able to turn these weaknesses into strengths. Each person was assigned a task, and as we progressed with the project, we changed tools because they were more practical or better suited to our work. Initially, Pablo and David used Requests for programming, the first step being to convert everything to Perlin noise, hoping that this would be easier to adapt to sound. Sebastian worked on photographic analysis and was introduced to spectrograms. The difficulty arose between using grayscale and RGB. Sebastian, being a photographer, opted for grayscale, believing it would be easier to translate. There were several communication problems, mainly due to our limited knowledge of Perlin noise and its compatibility.

So we decided to take two approaches. Pablo would create the Perlin noise, while Sebastian would edit the original images, initially in Photo Pea and later in Pixlr. This was to define the sound's amplitude. For example, a light gray might represent a high amplitude, while a darker gray might represent a lower amplitude. This aspect was defined by Luis, who has experience in music and acoustics. David, for his part, was in charge of the interface and website, that is, the overall presentation of the project. In the end, we chose to create eight images, including those of ocean currents, winds, and the amount of certain gases in the Earth's atmosphere. The latter, such as O3 and CO, didn't need editing, only definition. The image format was DPI.

The second day of NASA Space Apps focused primarily on creating the audio tracks in Reaper and the Streamlit website for presentations. There would be between two and three audio tracks per image: one for the grayscale image (although it was displayed in color, it was processed in Reaper in the planned format), another for the Perlin noise, and in some cases, the silhouette tracks, which would be in black and white only, without grayscale. It was a more demanding day, but the team was prepared, as everyone leveraged their skills. We also received training outside the event on functions like Python programming, which was challenging for David, who encountered difficulties with the interface, one of the most difficult aspects to implement, but which we ultimately executed effectively.

Regarding the image-to-sound conversion, as mentioned previously, we used Photo Pea to edit the image. Luis then used a spectrogram to synthesize the image and convert it into music using parameters he defined, such as frequency and amplitude. In conclusion, while our project didn't achieve the expected outcome, it allowed us to explore the team's skills related to the global issues that NASA addresses. It enabled us to learn to use programs we hadn't previously encountered, test new perspectives, analyze data in different ways, and, above all, create something extraordinary that, in part, represents a future concept that could help people with visual impairments identify graphics using sound. Additionally, we gained experience in areas such as Python programming and Perlin noise, which could be considered the greatest success and most enriching experience we could have had with this challenge: the opportunity to learn while complementing each other for the common good.
